title: What 'Excellent Condition' Actually Means (Photos Don't Lie)
meta_description: Greasy handprints sold as 'excellent'? Here's what condition grades actually mean and how to spot sellers who tell the truth about phone quality.
content:
What 'Excellent Condition' Actually Means (Photos Don't Lie)

A customer just complained about getting a phone with "greasy handprints" that was sold as "excellent condition." That's not excellent. That's not even good.

Here's the problem: every seller calls their phones "excellent" because it sounds better than "decent" or "fair." But words matter when you're spending $400 on a device.

The Grade Inflation Problem

Walk into any refurb seller's warehouse and you'll see the same thing. Phones with scratches marked "excellent." Devices with loose charging ports labeled "like new." Pictures that hide the damage under perfect lighting.

Why? Because "excellent" sells faster than "good," and "good" sells faster than "fair." So everyone grades up.

But what happens when you get the phone? You feel cheated. Because excellent should mean excellent.

What Each Grade Actually Means

Excellent: Looks new from arm's length. 90%+ battery health. Screen is spotless. No visible wear on the body. Works perfectly in every way.

Good: Light scratches you only see up close. 85%+ battery health. Everything functions perfectly. Shows it was used but not abused.

Fair: Visible wear, deeper scratches, maybe a small ding. 80%+ battery health. All features work but it clearly looks used.

That's it. No fancy marketing terms. No "like-new premium grade A+" nonsense.

90%+ battery health, spotless screen, looks new from normal distance.

How We Actually Grade Phones

Every phone gets the same 65-point inspection. Screen test under bright light. Battery diagnostics with real cycle counts. Camera tests in different lighting. Charging port tested with multiple cables.

If there's a scratch, we photograph it. If the battery is 87%, we show 87% — not "excellent battery life." If Face ID has issues, we mark it down or fix it.

Because when you get the phone, it should match exactly what we described. No surprises.

Red Flags to Watch For

Stock photos instead of actual device photos. Vague condition descriptions like "shows minimal wear." No battery health percentage listed. Phrases like "fully tested" without specifics.

And the biggest red flag? When excellent-grade phones cost the same as good-grade phones elsewhere. Real excellent condition phones cost more because they're rarer.

Light scratches, 86% battery health, perfect functionality at honest price.

Why Honest Grading Matters

Look, nobody wants to pay excellent prices for good condition. But nobody wants to pay good prices and get fair condition either.

Honest grading means you get exactly what you expect. Our return rate is under 3% because the phone you receive matches the photos and description exactly.

That's how it should work. No greasy handprints. No surprise scratches. No inflated grades.

Just the condition grade that matches what you actually get.

mainEntity.name: What does excellent condition mean for refurbished phones?

acceptedAnswer.text: Excellent condition means the phone looks new from arm's length with 90%+ battery health, spotless screen, no visible wear on the body, and perfect functionality in all features.

mainEntity.name: How can I tell if a seller is honest about phone condition?

acceptedAnswer.text: Look for actual device photos (not stock images), specific battery health percentages, detailed condition descriptions, and realistic pricing that reflects true condition grades.

mainEntity.name: Why do some refurbished phones have greasy handprints but are sold as excellent?

acceptedAnswer.text: Grade inflation - sellers mark up condition grades because 'excellent' sells faster than 'good.' Honest sellers clean devices thoroughly and grade accurately based on actual condition.
